name: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy plus / dystonia (LHON-plus)
aliases: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy plus dystonia

reference.source: GeneReviews Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: LHON-plus denotes the optic neuropathy of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy accompanied by extraocular features, most characteristically dystonia and other movement or neurological disorders
The visual component is a subacute, painless, usually sequential bilateral central visual loss from optic nerve degeneration, typically in young adult men
It is maternally inherited, caused by mitochondrial DNA point mutations affecting complex I subunits, classically m.11778G>A, m.3460G>A and m.14484T>C
Incomplete penetrance and a strong male predominance mean many mutation carriers never lose vision, and additional environmental factors such as tobacco and alcohol modify risk
In LHON-plus, dystonia often reflects bilateral striatal (putaminal) lesions, and MRI may show basal ganglia signal change
Some pedigrees combine optic neuropathy with dystonia and additional features resembling other mitochondrial or extrapyramidal syndromes

Management is supportive with low-vision rehabilitation, avoidance of mitochondrial toxins including tobacco and excess alcohol, and generic use of quinone-based cofactor therapy under specialist guidance
reference.pathophysiology: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy results from maternally inherited point mutations in mitochondrial DNA that encode subunits of respiratory-chain complex I, impairing electron transport, reducing ATP synthesis and increasing reactive oxygen species. Retinal ganglion cells, whose small unmyelinated axons in the papillomacular bundle have high energy demand, are selectively vulnerable, leading to their degeneration and central visual loss. In LHON-plus the same energy failure and oxidative stress extend to other high-demand neurons, particularly in the basal ganglia, producing dystonia and additional neurological features; the reasons some carriers develop the extended phenotype relate to mutant load, nuclear and mitochondrial genetic background, hormonal factors and environmental exposures.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated classic Leber hereditary optic neuropathy without extraocular features
Dominant optic atrophy (OPA1) and other hereditary optic neuropathies
Primary dystonia syndromes and Wilson disease
Leigh syndrome and other complex I mitochondrial disorders
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing for the common LHON mitochondrial DNA mutations with heteroplasmy assessment
Ophthalmological evaluation including visual fields, colour vision and optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer
Brain MRI to assess basal ganglia and optic pathway involvement
Visual evoked potentials to document optic nerve dysfunction
Blood lactate and, where indicated, muscle respiratory-chain enzymology
Assessment for modifiable risk factors including tobacco and alcohol use
redFlags: Rapidly progressive bilateral visual loss requiring urgent specialist assessment
New or worsening generalised dystonia impairing function
Additional bulbar or extrapyramidal deterioration suggesting a broader mitochondrial syndrome
Continued exposure to mitochondrial toxins during acute visual decline
reference.prognosis: Visual prognosis is generally poor with most affected individuals reaching legal blindness, though the m.14484T>C mutation carries a better chance of partial recovery; when dystonia and other extraocular features are present the neurological disability tends to persist and may progress.
pitfalls: Assuming carriers will inevitably lose vision, ignoring the marked incomplete penetrance and sex bias
Overlooking dystonia and basal ganglia lesions that distinguish LHON-plus from isolated LHON
Failing to counsel about maternal inheritance and avoidance of tobacco and alcohol
Misattributing subacute visual loss to optic neuritis and delaying mitochondrial testing
management: Consider idebenone to support residual vision, and advise avoidance of tobacco and alcohol as recognised aggravators
Manage dystonia symptomatically with agents such as anticholinergics, baclofen, a trial of levodopa, or focal botulinum toxin injections
Consider deep brain stimulation for disabling, medically refractory dystonia in appropriate patients
Provide visual rehabilitation and low-vision aids alongside physiotherapy and occupational therapy for motor disability
Monitor visual and neurological status with ophthalmic imaging, perimetry and neuroimaging of the basal ganglia
Offer genetic counselling for maternal mitochondrial inheritance with heteroplasmy assessment and evaluation of maternal relatives
Coordinate care through mitochondrial medicine, movement-disorder neurology and neuro-ophthalmology
